lesson.title: Holding the Middle Ground: Stabilizing Selection
lesson.summary: Stabilizing selection favors individuals with intermediate, average phenotypes over those at either extreme, narrowing a population's range of variation without shifting where its average sits.
lesson.body:
Natural selection does not always act in the same direction, and the shape of a trait's distribution across a population reveals a great deal about how selection is currently acting on it. This section, along with directional and disruptive selection covered next, describes the three basic patterns selection can take when acting on a trait that varies continuously across a population, such as height, weight, or coloration intensity, each defined by which part of the trait's distribution has the highest relative fitness. Stabilizing selection is the pattern in which individuals near the middle of the distribution have the highest relative fitness, while individuals at both extremes are selected against. The result, generation after generation, is a population whose average value for the trait stays roughly where it was, but whose spread around that average narrows, because the tails of the distribution are being trimmed from both sides at once.

Human birth weight is the textbook example, and walking through why makes the logic concrete. Babies born significantly underweight tend to have underdeveloped lungs and other organs and face higher rates of complications shortly after birth. Babies born significantly overweight face a different set of risks, particularly difficulties during delivery itself. Babies born at a weight near the population average face neither problem as severely, and historically have shown the lowest rates of complications and mortality. The result is a birth weight distribution that clusters tightly around an intermediate value, not because some optimal weight was designed in advance, but because, generation after generation, both the too small and the too large tails of the distribution have faced worse outcomes than the middle. Notice what is not happening here: the average birth weight is not increasing or decreasing over time the way it would under directional selection. The distribution simply stays centered while narrowing.

At the level of allele frequency, stabilizing selection tends to work against fixation. Where directional selection, discussed next, pushes an allele toward 100 percent or 0 percent because one extreme phenotype is consistently favored, stabilizing selection favors combinations of alleles that produce an intermediate phenotype, which often means keeping multiple alleles at moderate, stable frequencies rather than eliminating any of them outright. This is also the most common of the three selection patterns in nature for traits that already sit near a stable optimum. Once a population is well matched to a fairly constant environment, most deviation in either direction tends to be disadvantageous, which is exactly the condition stabilizing selection thrives on maintaining.
